meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nobody goes there anymore. It's too crowded'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Yogi Berra original: the gag appeared anonymously in 1907 and in a 1943 New Yorker story. He was first credited in 1962.

answer.label: Not original to Yogi Berra — a joke that predates him
answer.authorDates: Earliest known version printed December 1907 · author unidentified
answer.sourceLine: The paradox was already a stock newspaper gag decades before Berra was famous: Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to an anonymous 1907 humor column, and the modern wording — “Nobody goes there any more. It’s too crowded.” — appears in John McNulty’s New Yorker story of 20 February 1943, spoken by a taxicab driver. Berra was not credited with it in print until 1962, though he later said he had said it, about Ruggeri’s in St. Louis.
answer.confidenceText: He may well have said it — but he did not coin it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “Sparklets” humor column, New York newspaper, December 1907 — author unidentified
Some Nights When Nothing Happens Are the Best Nights in This Place
The New Yorker, 20 February 1943, p. 13, by John McNulty

source.excerpt:
1907, anonymous: “Oh, don’t go there on Saturday; it’s so frightfully crowded! Nobody goes there then!”

1943, spoken by a taxicab driver in John McNulty’s New Yorker story: “Nobody goes there any more. It’s too crowded.”
trail: December 1907 — the earliest strong match appears anonymously in a New York humor column called “Sparklets” and is reprinted in other papers over the next several years, per Quote Investigator ↗.

20 February 1943 — John McNulty’s New Yorker story “Some Nights When Nothing Happens Are the Best Nights in This Place” gives the modern wording to a New York hackman; McNulty wrote for the magazine from 1937 until his death in 1956 (Wikipedia ↗).
1962 — the Cleveland Plain Dealer becomes the first paper to put the joke in Yogi Berra’s mouth; Wikiquote ↗ notes it was “not attributed to Berra until 1962” and lists it as misattributed.

Later — Berra retold it as his own, about Ruggeri’s in St. Louis, and Wikipedia records the quip in that form (Wikipedia ↗) — the same article notes that at least one famous line credited to him, “It ain’t over till the fat lady sings,” was not his.
source.cutTag: Two printings, 36 years apart, neither of them Berra
source.excerptNote: Both passages are quoted from the chronology assembled by Quote Investigator; the 1943 line is the earliest documented instance of the wording the world now attaches to Yogi Berra.

source.rightsNote: No single author can be tied to this wording, so no clean rights status can be asserted. The anonymous 1907 newspaper version is long out of copyright, but the familiar phrasing is first documented in John McNulty’s New Yorker story of 20 February 1943 — a work first published after 1930 and therefore potentially still in copyright — and even there it is presented as an overheard saloon joke rather than an original coinage. Treat the line as an unattributed folk gag, not as public-domain text.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.kicker: The name the joke landed on
author.heading: Who was Yogi Berra?
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra was born in St. Louis in 1925 and died in 2015, having spent a 19-season Hall of Fame career in the majors — all but the last of it catching for the New York Yankees. He became at least as famous for his Yogi-isms — short, self-contradicting one-liners — as for the baseball, and the label eventually acted as a magnet: lines he never originated drifted onto his name because they sounded like him. Berra saw the problem himself, and it produced the most quoted Yogi-ism of all: “I really didn’t say everything I said.”

misattribution.heading: How it became a Yogi-ism
misattribution.intro: This is a floating joke — an anonymous newspaper gag that changed speakers every decade or so until it found a name famous enough to stay attached to.

items.who: A New York cabdriver in a 1943 New Yorker story
items.why: John McNulty’s story “Some Nights When Nothing Happens Are the Best Nights in This Place” (20 February 1943) gives the modern wording to a hackman — nineteen years before Berra was linked to it, per QI ↗.

items.who: Berra himself, retelling it as his
items.why: In The Yogi Book (1998) Berra told the story as his own — talking with Stan Musial and Joe Garagiola in 1959 about Ruggeri’s restaurant in his old St. Louis neighbourhood — as quoted by Quote Investigator ↗. That he repeated it is plausible; that he invented it is ruled out by the 1907 and 1943 printings.

misattribution.truthLine: A stock joke of the early 1900s, author unknown, that attached itself to Yogi Berra in 1962 and never let go — see Quote Investigator’s full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Yogi
lead: The line is a perfect little logic trap: it treats “nobody” as shorthand for “nobody worth counting” and then collides that with a literal reading. That shape — obviously wrong on the surface, obviously true underneath — is exactly the shape of a Yogi-ism, which is why the joke found its way to Berra rather than the other way around.

By the early 1960s Berra had become a kind of gravitational centre for paradoxical one-liners. Sportswriters needed a name to hang a good gag on; Berra was the name. He rarely fought it, and in his own books he told the story as his own, placing it at Ruggeri’s, a restaurant in his old St. Louis neighbourhood.
context.detailsSummary: The paper trail, decade by decade
detailsBody: December 1907 — the earliest strong match, in a New York humor column called “Sparklets”: “Oh, don’t go there on Saturday; it’s so frightfully crowded! Nobody goes there then!” No author named. It was reprinted in other papers over the following years.
1941 — a columnist reports comedian Rags Ragland crediting a version to Suzanne Ridgeway: “Now I know why nobody ever comes here; it’s too crowded.”

20 February 1943 — John McNulty’s New Yorker story “Some Nights When Nothing Happens Are the Best Nights in This Place” puts the modern wording in the mouth of a hackman. A sportswriter in the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette gives it to a stock Irishman that April.
1962 — the first newspaper attribution to Yogi Berra, in the Cleveland Plain Dealer. From there it becomes a fixed Yogi-ism.
context.pull: The joke did not come from Yogi Berra. It came to him.
